templates.pattern: An electron in a hydrogen atom is in energy level n = [N]. Calculate the energy of the electron in eV using the Bohr model. (En = −13.6 ÷ n² eV)
templates.explanation:
Energy of electron = −13.6 ÷ n²
= −13.6 ÷ [N]²
= −13.6 ÷ [N*N]
= [RESULT] eV

The negative sign indicates the electron is bound to the nucleus. Energy level n=1 is the ground state with the most negative — most stable — energy. Higher levels are less negative — less stable.

templates.pattern: An electron in hydrogen falls from energy level n = [N2] to n = [N1]. Calculate the energy of the photon emitted in eV. (En = −13.6 ÷ n² eV)
templates.explanation:
Energy of photon = E_lower − E_upper
= −13.6/[N1]² − (−13.6/[N2]²)
= 13.6 × (1/[N1]² − 1/[N2]²)
= 13.6 × (1/[N1*N1] − 1/[N2*N2])
= [RESULT] eV

When an electron falls to a lower energy level it emits a photon. The photon energy equals the difference between the two energy levels. This produces the characteristic emission spectrum of hydrogen.

templates.pattern: A photon has a frequency of [F] × 10¹⁴ Hz. Calculate the energy of the photon in joules. (h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s)
templates.explanation:
Photon energy E = hf
= 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × [F] × 10¹⁴
= 6.63 × [F] × 10⁻²⁰
= [RESULT] J

Photon energy is directly proportional to frequency. Ultraviolet photons have enough energy to cause chemical reactions and damage DNA. This is why UV radiation is harmful.

templates.pattern: A photon has an energy of [E] × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Calculate the wavelength of the photon in metres. (h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s, c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s)
templates.explanation:
From E = hc ÷ λ:
λ = hc ÷ E
= 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × 3 × 10⁸ ÷ ([E] × 10⁻¹⁹)
= 19.89 × 10⁻²⁶ ÷ [E] × 10⁻¹⁹
= [RESULT] m

Visible light has wavelengths between 400 nm and 700 nm. This formula connects the particle nature (energy) and wave nature (wavelength) of light.

templates.pattern: An electron of mass 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg moves at [V] × 10⁶ m/s. Calculate the de Broglie wavelength of the electron in metres. (h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s)
templates.explanation:
de Broglie wavelength λ = h ÷ mv
= 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ ÷ (9.11 × 10⁻³¹ × [V] × 10⁶)
= 6.63 ÷ (9.11 × [V] × 10³)
= [RESULT] m

The de Broglie wavelength shows that particles have wave properties. Electron diffraction experiments confirm this — electrons produce diffraction patterns just like waves.

templates.pattern: The first ionisation energy of element X is [IE] kJ/mol. Calculate the energy in joules required to ionise one atom of element X. (Avogadro's number = 6.02 × 10²³)
templates.explanation:
Energy per atom = IE ÷ Avogadro's number
= [IE] × 10³ ÷ 6.02 × 10²³
= [RESULT] J

Ionisation energies are given per mole. Dividing by Avogadro's number gives the energy to remove one electron from one atom.

templates.pattern: The first ionisation energy of lithium is 520 kJ/mol. Element X has atomic number [Z] and its first ionisation energy is [IE] kJ/mol. Calculate how many times greater the ionisation energy of element X is compared to lithium.
templates.explanation:
Ratio = IE of element X ÷ IE of lithium
= [IE] ÷ 520
= [RESULT]

First ionisation energies vary across the periodic table. Noble gases have the highest values. Alkali metals have the lowest. This ratio shows how much more tightly bound the outermost electron is compared to lithium.

templates.pattern: The [N]th ionisation energy of an element is [IE1] kJ/mol and the [N1]th ionisation energy is [IE2] kJ/mol. Calculate the ratio IE[N1] ÷ IE[N].
templates.explanation:
Ratio = IE[N1] ÷ IE[N]
= [IE2] ÷ [IE1]
= [RESULT]

A large ratio (greater than 3) suggests the next electron is removed from an inner shell — indicating the group number of the element equals [N].

templates.pattern: An element has two isotopes of masses [M1] and [M2]. The relative atomic mass is [RAM]. Calculate the percentage abundance of isotope 1.
templates.explanation:
From RAM = (M₁ × AB₁ + M₂ × AB₂) ÷ 100:
AB₁ + AB₂ = 100
Solving: AB₁ = (RAM × 100 − M₂ × 100) ÷ (M₁ − M₂)
= [RESULT]%

This is the reverse RAM calculation — finding abundance from the known RAM and isotope masses.

templates.pattern: A sample has a mass of [MASS] g. The relative molecular mass of the compound is [RMM]. Calculate the number of molecules in the sample. Give your answer as a multiple of 10²³. (Avogadro's number = 6.02 × 10²³)
templates.explanation:
Moles = mass ÷ RMM = [MASS] ÷ [RMM] = [MOLES] mol
Number of molecules = moles × Avogadro's number
= [MOLES] × 6.02 × 10²³
= [RESULT] × 10²³

This two-step calculation connects mass to number of particles — a fundamental skill in quantitative chemistry.
